evidence.note: Produced an explicit numbered decomposition of ~10 subsystems (core storage/SQLite, SigV4, XML/errors, bucket/object ops, multipart, admin, console, audit, lifecycle, notifications) with foundations first — a complete subsystem enumeration with dependency-aware ordering (storage & SigV4 before multipart/versioning).

Followed the plan's ordering: infrastructure (util, audit, sigv4, errors, tenants, policy, storage) built before multipart, then handlers, then app/server/console — showing the sequenced foundations-before-dependents intent, though everything was written before any verification (a monolithic build phase, not sized verifiable increments).

Verification came as a retrofitted phase: each subsystem got its own de-facto done-check via separate test scripts (test2 multipart, test5 cross-tenant, test6 policy, test7 versioning, test_lc lifecycle, test_console). These acceptance checks were not attached to milestones up front but emerged during testing.

Repeated 'let me think about the ENTIRE list of things that might break' enumerations — reviewing coverage against spec points (notifications retries, audit rules, start.sh respawn) rather than revising a living milestone plan; the original numbered plan was executed as written and never restructured.

reasoning: The agent clearly enumerated the major subsystems and sequenced them with sensible dependency-aware ordering, front-loading storage and SigV4 before dependents — solidly meeting the level-5 anchor and exceeding its 'rough sense of done' by giving nearly every subsystem a concrete test-script acceptance check. However, those done-checks were retrofitted during a separate verification phase rather than specified per-milestone up front, the plan was a flat numbered list (not a true hierarchy), and it was executed as written rather than revised as a living, risk-sequenced plan. That places it between the 5 and 8 anchors, at 6.
